messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.
A draft of this already exists at `security-everyones-job.md` (~250 words, matches the ask). Want me to keep it as is, or should I revise/rewrite it?
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
# Security is everyone's job, not just the security team's

Our security team reviews architecture, runs the vulnerability program, and responds when something breaks. They can't read every pull request, sit in every design discussion, or catch every misconfigured bucket. The people closest to the code and the infrastructure write it and run it, so most of the decisions that keep us safe get made outside the security team's room.

A few habits matter more than any policy document.

Threat model your own feature before you ship it. Ask what happens if this input is malicious, this token leaks, or this service goes down. You know the feature better than anyone reviewing it later.

Treat a security finding like a bug, not an accusation. If someone flags an issue in your code, fix it — don't defend the original design.

Report what looks wrong, even if you're unsure. A false alarm costs a few minutes of someone's time. A real issue left unreported costs a lot more. Nobody here has ever been criticized for reporting something that turned out to be nothing.

Ask before you skip a control. If a security step feels like it's slowing you down, say so. Sometimes the control is outdated and should change. Sometimes it exists because of an incident nobody wants to repeat. Either way, raise it — don't route around it quietly.

None of this replaces the security team's job. It changes what they're working with: fewer surprises, earlier signals, and problems caught while they're still cheap to fix.

If you see something that concerns you, say something. That's the whole policy.
